headline: Omatsuri is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 祭り (matsuri, “festival”).
Mezurashii ultimately comes from the verb 愛づ (medu), whose descendant 愛でる (mederu) means “to love; to admire”.
Dasu is the causative form of 出づ (idu): いだす (idasu) in Old Japanese.
Daigaku is from Middle Chinese 大學 (MC dajH haewk).
Kuraberu is the modern lower monograde descendant of an old lower bigrade verb, 比ぶ.
Hima is probably 間 (hi, “free time”) plus 間 (ma, “space, interval”), and the first may relate to 皹 (hibi, “chap of the skin”).
Sakiototoi is 先 (saki, “previous”) plus 一昨日 (ototoi, “day before yesterday”); the kanji spelling is jukujikun.
Koshi first appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *kəsi.
Mata is from Proto-Japonic *mata, cognate with Miyako and Okinawan mata.
Tsutome is the continuative stem of 勤める (tsutomeru).
Maru shifted from Old Japanese 丸 (maro), and is related to 麻呂 (maro).
Higeki is a calque of English tragedy, built from 悲 (hi, “sad, sorrowful”) plus 劇 (geki, “drama; play”).
Sumai is the continuative stem of 住まう (sumau, “to live at; to dwell; to reside”), first attested in the 970s.
Osameru is cognate with 治める (osameru) and 修める (osameru).
This kaeru, written 換, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the lower bigrade pattern.
Zōsen is Middle Chinese 造船.
Marugoto is 丸 (maru, “round; (by extension) entirety”) plus ごと (-goto).
Tobikomu is tobi, the stem of 飛ぶ (tobu, “to jump; to fly”), plus 込む (komu, “to go into”).
Chōjo is 長 (“long; elder”) plus 女 (“woman; female”).
Shū, “week”, is from Middle Chinese 周 (MC tsyuw).
Shizen kagaku is 自然 (shizen, “nature”) plus 科学 (kagaku, “science”).
Shōgi is first attested in the Shinsarugakuki (11th century) as 將基, and is probably cognate with Chinese 象棋 (xiàngqí).
Shi, “poem”, is from Middle Chinese 詩 (MC syi).
Sukī is borrowed from English ski, from Norwegian ski.
Dōmo is どう (dō, “how”) plus も (mo, “ever, even, also”): close in meaning to “no matter how”.
Iroiro is a reduplication of 色 (iro, “colour; type; kind”).
Shimekiri is the stem of 締め切る (shimekiru): 締め (shime, “fastening, locking, shutting”) plus 切り (kiri).
Ishiki is from Middle Chinese 意識 (ʔiH syik).
Hikidasu is hiki, the stem of 引く (hiku, “to pull”), plus 出す (dasu, “to take out”).
Sukima is 隙 (suki, “gap”) plus 間 (ma, “space”).
Tatoe is perhaps from たとい (tatoi).
